title: Bridging continuous control and Floquet driving for charging many-body spin chains
authors: Sebastián V. Romero, Xi Chen, Yue Ban
abstract: Recent advances in quantum information and quantum thermodynamics have reshaped the understanding of energy storage at the microscopic scale, paving the way toward protocols for storing and transferring energy in quantum devices. These systems, known as quantum batteries, offer a conceptual alternative to conventional macroscopic chemical batteries by exploiting quantum coherence, correlations, and many-body dynamics. By navigating the landscape of established spin-based quantum batteries, we review existing charging and work-extraction protocols, as well as the impact of external factors on their performance. Motivated by Floquet-engineered proposals, we further establish a connection between continuously and periodically driven spin chains as platforms for quantum energy storage. Finally, we survey experimental realizations and proposals, highlighting their implementability and scalability in current and near-term quantum technologies.
summary: This work reviews the concept of quantum batteries, focusing on how many-body spin chains can store energy beyond classical limits. It develops a theoretical framework connecting continuous external driving to discrete Floquet driving protocols using models like the kicked-Ising chain. The paper is significant for understanding achievable quantum enhancements in energy storage devices.
main_problem: The paper reviews quantum batteries (QBs) and establishes a theoretical connection between continuous control and periodically driven Floquet systems for enhancing energy storage.
main_result: Quantum effects, particularly those leveraging coherence in spin chains, can lead to superextensive scaling of charging power beyond classical limits. The framework connects these two driving regimes via the kicked-Ising model.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis involving time evolution operators (Floquet formalism) and diagnostic tools like ergotropy to quantify energy storage capabilities.
model_or_system: The primary system is many-body spin chains modeled as quantum batteries, utilizing Hamiltonians for both the battery ($H_b$) and the charging mechanism ($H_c$). Specific models include the Ising chain and SYK models.
key_observables: Quantum Charging Advantage (Superextensive Scaling $P(	au^*) \sim N^{1+\ell}$), Ergotropy, Maximum Mean Charging Power $P(	au)$.
important_parameters: Interaction range ($g_{ij}$ decay), anisotropy ($\alpha$), and the nature of driving (continuous vs. periodic/kicked).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes an infinite energy reservoir for charging protocols, and the comparison between continuous and Floquet limits is central.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares the performance of a spin-chain QB under continuous driving versus optimal periodic kicking (quasikick).
paper_structure: The paper reviews existing QB protocols, develops the connection between continuous control and Floquet engineering using spin chains, analyzes scaling laws based on interaction range, and concludes by surveying experimental realizations.
why_interesting: It directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and energy storage in quantum systems, bridging concepts from quantum information (coherence) with condensed matter dynamics (spin chains).

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Schematic of an Ising-chain QB bridging continuously driven and periodically kicked transverse- field charging protocols. From lighter to darker blue, the injected energy in a QB (top) under charging protocols with decreasing pulse width (bottom). While a continuous drive (represented by a constant line) yields a poor performance, a periodically-kicked pulse (depicted with arrows) reaches maximal charging without fluctuations. Between these two limiting cases, a finite-width periodic pulse coined as quasikick [42] (dashed line), displays a performance lying between both limit regimes.
